newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa govt says Telkom privatisation on track.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa govt says Telkom privatisation on track.

text.p: South Africa's Post and Telecommunications Minister Jay Naidoo said on Thursday that the government planned to issue Telkom with a licence granting an exclusivity period of five years for fixed-line voice services.

Naidoo said the government had prepared three draft licences, due to come into effect from April, for the previously unlicensed state telecommunications giant, guaranteeing it exclusive rights in this key part of the market.
The publication of the draft licences, which are now subject to public comment, is an important step in preparing for the partial privatisation of Telkom.
Naidoo said he expected to receive financial bids from overseas companies looking to take a stake of up to 30 percent in the company by early March.
"We expect that by the beginning of March we will have received financial bids," Naidoo told reporters via video link from Cape Town.
The government has shortlisted four potential bidders to take a strategic equity stake of 20 to 30 percent in Telkom.
SBC Communications Inc and Telekom Malaysia Bhd have said they intend to bid jointly, and Deutsche Telekom AG and France Telecom are widely expected to do likewise.

Naidoo said the basic exclusivity period for fixed-line services would be five years under the draft licence proposals, but Telkom and its strategic equity partner could apply for another year of exclusivity if they achieved certain targets.
Foreign companies would enter bids to increase rollout targets as part of the overall bidding process for a stake in Telkom.

Current demand for new telephones in South Africa is put at 1.8 million lines over the next five years. But Naidoo said he was convinced demand would be higher than this and the government hoped a partly privatised Telkom would achieve greater penetration of previously deprived areas.

Should the company achieve 90 percent of its total new lines rollout target within the first four years and commit itself to rolling out a total of three million lines it could be eligible for the extra year of exclusivity, Naidoo said.

Naidoo would not be drawn on the likely value of the sale of the stake in Telkom, which marks the government's first major step in the promised restructuring of state-owned assets inherited from the apartheid era.
Industry sources say the deal is likely to value Telkom at over $4 billion, making its sub-Sahara Africa's biggest privatisation.
